assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new observational window: the IceCube detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (2013), followed by the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations, created neutrino astronomy and addresses the origin of cosmic rays. It is a km3 detector built in Antarctic ice, the kind of instrument-driven discovery I weigh most heavily.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube and Spiering was a central figure in the AMANDA/Baikal/IceCube development; the supplied credit supports a two-person prize. The collaboration is large and other pioneers of the field (e.g. earlier DUMAND and Baikal efforts, the IceCube spokespeople) could be argued for, so allocation is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation of the diffuse flux is partly from ANTARES and later KM3NeT/Baikal-GVD results, though the strongest source associations rest largely on IceCube alone. Recognition is timely, with the field now mature enough to be stable.
uncertainties: Source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are statistically moderate and not yet independently confirmed at high significance.
Whether the prize should name instrument builders or the analysts who made the discovery is unresolved; I am not independently verifying the fine details of the credit history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: First horizon-scale images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) are a landmark measurement achieved by a global mm-VLBI array, with calibration and systematics handled with great care. It gives direct strong-field evidence on black holes and complements the 2020 prize.
assessment.attribution: Doeleman led the EHT, Falcke proposed imaging the shadow and Moran drove mm-VLBI technique and instrumentation; this is a plausible three-person configuration. The EHT is a collaboration of hundreds, so any selection of three will be contested.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets and multi-epoch consistency lend confidence, but the interpretation of image details (spin, jet launching, ring morphology) is still developing.
uncertainties: Image reconstruction depends on priors and pipeline choices; the community debate on reconstruction fidelity is not fully closed.
Large-collaboration attribution is a real obstacle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via the magic-wavelength idea and its realisation, reach 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and enable tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. This is precision instrumentation of the highest order, with a clear lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock concept; Ye brought it to record precision and applications. The two-name credit is clean, though other clock groups (e.g. Strontium work at JILA and elsewhere, Hg, Yb) also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce and compare clocks at the 10^-18 level, and the redefinition of the second is under active discussion. Timely and mature.
uncertainties: The role of ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) and other groups in the overall story could be argued to complicate a lattice-clock-only prize.
I am relying on my general knowledge for the credit history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (superfluid to Mott transition, quantum gas microscopes, Hubbard physics) is a broad and influential experimental platform that follows from the BEC recognition of 2001. Outside my own expertise, so I defer to colleagues on depth, but the importance and breadth are clear.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Cirac supplied the theoretical proposals (with Jaksch et al.), Bloch and Greiner the decisive Mott-insulator and microscope experiments, and Esslinger the fermionic work. Five names are credited; three must be chosen and Greiner or Esslinger exclusion is a real difficulty. Choosing the theorists plus Bloch is one defensible configuration.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated across many laboratories, now a mature field. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Theory-plus-experiment split and the exclusion of Greiner and Esslinger remain unresolved.
Whether simulation results yet exceed classical capability is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and pixel detectors transformed particle tracking and vertexing and underpin discoveries of heavy flavour and the Higgs boson, as well as medical and space applications. As a detector builder I regard this as a clear case of an invention enabling discoveries, in the spirit of the Charpak prize.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer introduced planar processing for detectors, Heijne the hybrid pixel concept and Parker the microstrip and 3D developments; the supplied credit fits a three-way split. Others (e.g. the CERN RD19 groups, CCD developers) also have claims.
assessment.maturity: Ubiquitous and independently proven over four decades; the technology is fully mature. The question is whether the Committee views detector inventions as sufficiently physics-driven.
uncertainties: Competing claims from other pioneers (e.g. monolithic pixels, CCD vertex detectors) could dilute credit.
Prizes for instrumentation may be seen as lower priority than physics discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fast radio bursts, discovered in archival Parkes data in 2007, are a new class of extragalactic transient, now localised to galaxies and tied to magnetars via the galactic burst of SGR 1935+2154. They are a probe of the intergalactic medium and a rich puzzle.
assessment.attribution: Lorimer led the discovery paper with McLaughlin and Bailes; the discovery credit is relatively clear but later confirmation (Thornton et al. 2013) and CHIME/ASKAP localisations by others are also decisive for establishing the phenomenon.
assessment.maturity: Class existence is firmly confirmed, but the physical origin is still unsettled, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Emission mechanism and progenitors remain debated.
The discovery paper alone did not establish an extragalactic origin; later contributors are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping of antihydrogen and precise tests of CPT and gravity with antimatter, along with antiproton and positron magnetic moment measurements, push fundamental symmetry tests to extreme precision. Given my antimatter work with PAMELA I appreciate the technical difficulty and its relevance.
assessment.attribution: Hangst led ALPHA, which trapped and spectroscopically studied antihydrogen; Gabrielse led ATRAP and made the key precision lepton and antiproton measurements. Other contributors (e.g. the ATHENA team, Doser at AEgIS) complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: Results are accumulating but no violation of CPT has been seen, and independent cross-checks between ALPHA, ASACUSA and ATRAP are ongoing. Reasonably mature but the discovery narrative is a null-result precision story.
uncertainties: Absence of a discovery may reduce Nobel appeal.
Credit for first antihydrogen production (ATHENA/ATRAP) is separate from trapping.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (theory in 2011, correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018) launched twistronics and a vast field of moiré quantum matter. Outside my expertise, but the impact is exceptional, and I would rely on condensed-matter colleagues for the verdict.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states. The theory and experiment pairing is natural; Cory Dean's hBN work and others are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups, though interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is unsettled. Timely but still evolving.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and phase diagram remain debated.
Other groups (e.g. Dean, Yankowitz, and the Kim group) also contributed key results; I am not certain of the full credit history.
